opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing is that you have to give researchers a lot of freedom and a long time horizon. Breakthrough research doesn't come from people who are told, "You need to deliver this product feature in six months." It comes from people who are allowed to work on problems they find deeply interesting, sometimes for years, without being sure it's going to pay off.

When we created FAIR, one of the principles we insisted on was openness. Researchers publish their work, they release code, they collaborate with academia. Some people in industry think this is giving away the crown jewels, but it's actually the opposite. First, it's the only way to attract the best scientists, because their career depends on recognition from the community. If you tell them they can't publish, the best ones won't come. Second, research done in the open gets scrutinized and improved by the whole community, and progress goes faster for everyone, including you. Nobody has a monopoly on good ideas.

The second thing is to separate research from product development, but not too much. You need a buffer so researchers aren't pulled into short-term firefighting, but you also need channels so that when something works, it can be transferred to product groups. At Meta, things like PyTorch came out of that kind of environment, and it's had enormous impact both inside the company and outside.

Third, you need research leadership that understands science. Managers who are themselves researchers and who can tell the difference between a project that's failing and one that's just hard. You evaluate people on the quality and impact of their ideas over time, not on quarterly metrics.

And finally, you have to accept that a lot of what you fund won't work. That's the nature of research. If everything you try succeeds, you're not being ambitious enough. The companies that can afford to take that long-term view, and are wise enough to do it, are the ones that end up producing the breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers need to publish and explains that preventing publication would deter top scientists and slow community scrutiny and progress.

r002.rationale: It recommends research leaders who understand science and can distinguish a difficult project from a failing one, but does not clearly recommend hiring researchers with strong judgment about which problems to pursue.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends giving researchers freedom to pursue problems they find interesting over a long time horizon, without short-term product demands.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that research is not something you can direct from the top. You cannot tell people "go invent the next big thing." That's not how it works. What you can do is create the conditions under which good people, left to their own devices, will produce things that nobody expected.

So when we started FAIR at Facebook back in 2013, the model we had in mind was something like Bell Labs in its heyday, or Xerox PARC, or even the early days of Microsoft Research. The ingredients are fairly simple to state and very hard to actually implement.

The first is that you have to hire people who are intrinsically motivated. People who would do research anyway, whether you paid them or not, because they are obsessed with a question. And then you have to get out of their way. That means no micromanagement, no quarterly deliverables, no "what product is this going to ship in." If you ask that question too early, you kill the thing before it exists.

The second is openness. This is something I fought for very hard, and it was not obvious to everyone at the time. Researchers need to publish. They need to go to conferences, release code, talk to their peers at other institutions. If you lock everything up as secret, two things happen. First, you cannot attract the best people, because the best people want their work to be seen and to have impact on the field. And second, you lose the feedback loop. Science is a collective enterprise. Your ideas get better because other people poke holes in them. A lab that doesn't publish is a lab that's slowly drifting away from the frontier, and it doesn't even know it.

And honestly, this also serves the company. The whole field advances faster when things are open, and a company whose business depends on that technology benefits from the field advancing. PyTorch is a good example. We released it, the whole community adopted it, and that made everything we did internally better.

The third thing is that you need a long time horizon and leadership that understands this. When I took the job, the condition I set with Mark was essentially: research must be open, I will not be reporting through the product organization, and you have to accept that most of what we do will not pay off for years, if ever. He agreed, and he kept his word. Without that kind of commitment from the top, a research lab gets slowly absorbed into engineering, which is a different activity with different rhythms.

Now, that doesn't mean research should be completely disconnected. The way we organized it was that there's a continuum. You have people doing very fundamental work, and then there are groups that take promising results and push them toward something usable, and then product teams pick things up from there. The transition is gradual. But the crucial thing is that the pressure flows in one direction only. The fundamental research people are not being pulled by product deadlines.

And I'll add one more thing, which is about ambition. You have to encourage people to work on hard problems with the risk of failure. If you reward only incremental progress, that's all you'll get. Some of the most important things in deep learning came out of people pursuing ideas that the mainstream thought were dead ends. Including, I would say, deep learning itself, for a good portion of the 1990s and 2000s. So the atmosphere has to tolerate being wrong for a long time, as long as the reasons for pursuing the idea are sound.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers need to publish and warns that locking research up as secret harms hiring, feedback, and progress toward the frontier.

r002.rationale: It recommends hiring intrinsically motivated researchers who are obsessed with a question, but does not clearly recommend selecting researchers for strong judgment about which problems to pursue.

r003.rationale: It recommends getting out of researchers’ way, with no micromanagement or early product pressure, so they can pursue their work autonomously.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to give researchers the freedom to work on problems whose answers you don’t already know. If you can specify the result in advance, and say exactly when it will be delivered, you’re probably talking about development rather than research.

An industry lab needs a portfolio. Some projects can be close to applications, but others should be pursuing ideas that might not work, or might take several years to become useful. And those projects need protection from the pressure to produce something for the next product cycle. Otherwise, everyone gravitates toward incremental improvements, because those are easier to justify.

You also need an open intellectual environment. People should be able to publish, exchange ideas, challenge each other, and interact with the broader research community. That’s part of how you attract strong researchers, but it’s also how you make the research better.

The role of management is to provide resources, identify important questions, and bring together people with complementary skills. You can have a clear scientific ambition without prescribing every step. You can’t schedule a breakthrough, but you can create conditions in which people have a reasonable chance of producing one.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should be able to publish, but does not identify restrictions on publishing as an impediment to breakthrough research.

r002.rationale: It says management should identify important questions, but does not recommend hiring researchers with strong judgment about which problems to pursue.

r003.rationale: It recommends giving researchers freedom to pursue problems and says management should not prescribe every step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to give researchers the freedom to pursue ideas that might not work. If every project has to justify itself by a product launch six months from now, you’re going to get incremental improvements. You’re unlikely to get a breakthrough.

An industry lab has to have a longer horizon. You hire good people, give them resources, and let them work on questions they think are important. That doesn’t mean there’s no direction. You can have an ambitious goal, but you shouldn’t prescribe every step toward it.

And you need an atmosphere where people can exchange ideas, criticize each other’s work, and publish. Research benefits enormously from being connected to the broader scientific community. The management challenge is to protect that openness and that freedom, including when the work takes longer than expected or goes in a direction you didn’t anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response supports publishing and openness, but does not identify restrictions on publishing as an impediment to breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It recommends hiring “good people” and letting them choose important questions, but does not clearly say to hire researchers for their judgment about which problems to pursue.

r003.rationale: It recommends giving researchers freedom to pursue their ideas and says managers should not prescribe every step.
